### E. Prepayment, Lockout and Yield Maintenance

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
**E-1 (High) — Your proposed formula deletes the Term Sheet's 1.00% minimum premium.**
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Source:* Term Sheet §4.2 (premium "equal to the greater of (a) one percent (1.00%) of the outstanding principal balance … or (b) the present value of the excess …"); your §5 drafting instruction (formula with "In no event shall the Yield Maintenance Premium be less than zero" and no 1% floor).
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Analysis:* The two are not the same instrument. A pure yield-maintenance formula with a zero floor produces **no** premium whenever Treasury yields have risen above the note rate, which is precisely when a borrower most wants to prepay and when the lender's reinvestment loss is most acute from the borrower's perspective (the lender gains nothing, but loses a high-coupon asset). The 1% floor is the Term Sheet's protection against that outcome. Deleting it unilaterally would be a departure from a binding commitment and, in my view, not something an associate should make without instruction — particularly where Term Sheet §14.3 provides that the Loan Documents control in the event of conflict, which means a Borrower's counsel could argue that the deletion is evidence of the parties' agreed construction.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Resolution adopted:* I drafted the premium as the **greater of** 1.00% of the principal prepaid and the yield-maintenance amount, with the yield-maintenance leg floored at zero (Mortgage §13.3), and applied the same greater-of test to any prepayment accepted during the Lockout Period (§13.1). Please confirm, or direct that the floor be deleted and that the Term Sheet be amended in writing to match.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
**E-2 (High) — The 50 basis point placement is genuinely ambiguous, and the drafted formula does not replicate the Term Sheet's mechanics.**
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Source:* Term Sheet §4.2(b): the present value of the excess of (i) interest that would have accrued at the **Note rate**, over (ii) interest that would accrue "at the **treasury rate plus fifty (50) basis points**," discounted "at the treasury rate." Your instruction: add the 50 bps to the **loan rate** (i.e., the payment stream), with the spread reflecting the lender's bargained-for return.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Analysis:* These are two different formulas, not two readings of one formula. The Term Sheet computes an **interest differential** (Note rate versus Treasury + 50 bp, discounted at Treasury). Your instruction produces the market-standard **present value of remaining payments less principal** (payments at the Note rate, discounted at Treasury). On the Term Sheet's literal text the comparison uses Treasury + 50 bp as the comparison yield; on your instruction the 50 bp never enters the discount computation at all, because the Note rate already embeds the 285 bp spread. Both are defensible; they produce different numbers; and the Term Sheet's own internal logic (why compare to Treasury + 50 if the note rate is Treasury + 285?) favours your reading as the commercial intention, while the text favours the literal reading.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
*Resolution adopted:* I drafted your formula — PV of all remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest at the Note rate (without the Default Rate) through the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, discounted monthly at the Treasury Rate, less the outstanding principal prepaid, floored at zero, with the final payment adjusted for unamortized principal, and with the Treasury Rate defined by reference to FRB Statistical Release H.15, maturity matched to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, with linear interpolation and a fallback to the most recent prior publication (Mortgage §§1.1, 13.3). The formula is self-contained, deterministic and objectively calculable, which is the enforceability point you asked me to protect. *Recommendation:* **client decision required.** Obtain Marcus's written confirmation of the intended formula and, because the drafted formula does not track Term Sheet §4.2(b), either (i) a written confirmation/amendment of the Term Sheet by the Bank, or (ii) conform the drafting to the Term Sheet's literal mechanics. I would not put the form out without one of the two.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
**E-3 (Medium) — Lockout versus priced prepayment.** Term Sheet §4.1 prohibits prepayment during months 1–24 (in whole or in part) but then says any prepayment in violation "shall be subject to a prepayment premium as described in Section 4.2." A prohibition with a price is not a prohibition; it is an option, and the inconsistency also invites a penalty challenge (if the Bank must accept the money, the premium is not liquidated damages for a breach). *Resolution adopted:* I drafted the Lockout as an **absolute prohibition** with no prepayment right, coupled with a Lender election (in its sole and absolute discretion) to accept a tender at the greater of 1% and the yield-maintenance amount computed as though the prepayment occurred in the Yield Maintenance Period (§13.1). That preserves the Bank's position without creating a borrower right. Please confirm.
:::

::: {custom-style="Body Text"}
**E-4 (Medium) — Involuntary prepayments.** The Term Sheet is silent on whether casualty proceeds and condemnation awards applied to the Loan during the lockout or yield-maintenance period bear a premium. I drafted them as applied **at par** with no premium (§§10.4, 10.5, 13.6), which is the majority market position and is required for insurability (the title insurer and casualty carrier both assume restoration or par application), but you flagged that some lenders charge. *Recommendation:* confirm with Marcus; if the Bank wants a premium on involuntary prepayments, it must also accept that the insurer's restoration analysis becomes more complex and that the Borrower will resist.
:::

::: **E-5 (Medium) — Treasury Rate tenor.** Your instruction matches the reference maturity to the **last day of the Yield Maintenance Period** (approximately month 48, i.e., a 2-year reference at the start of the period). Market practice for this structure is often to match the remaining term to **maturity** (a 5-year reference at origination, declining), which produces a higher (longer-tenor) reference rate and hence a lower premium in a normal curve. The choice is a commercial one with a real dollar effect. *Resolution adopted:* matched to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, per your instruction, defined with interpolation. *Recommendation:* confirm; this is the kind of variable that, left undefined, produces the indefiniteness challenge you are trying to avoid.

The drafted clause is built for enforceability: a single defined reference rate and publication, a stated maturity-matching convention, interpolation, monthly discounting, an adjustment for unamortized principal, a floor, a conclusive-calculation provision, and an express liquidated-damages characterization (§13.7), plus a severability clause preserving the parties' intent if a component fails (§18.4). The cure available under this Section is as follows: Mortgagor may deposit into the DSCR Cure Reserve an amount (the "**Cure Amount**") equal to the excess, if any, of (a) Annual Debt Service for the applicable Measurement Period, over (b) the quotient obtained by dividing Net Operating Income for such Measurement Period by 1.25; such that, after treating the Cure Amount as a reduction of Annual Debt Service for such Measurement Period, the DSCR for such Measurement Period equals not less than 1.25x. I-1 (High) — The Phase I condition precedent cannot be satisfied on its
face, but the Bank has already waived Phase II.

Source: Term Sheet §12.1(c) requires a Phase I “indicating no recognized
environmental conditions requiring remediation or further investigation.” Phase
I ESA §4 identifies no RECs but one CREC on Lot 7; §6 records that “Calverley
Heritage Bank has waived the Phase II Environmental Site Assessment
requirement for this transaction based on the CREC status, the issuance of the
SCDHEC NFA letter, and the existence of the recorded institutional controls,”
documented in correspondence dated January 22, 2025 between Marcus
Prideaux and Clearfield.

Analysis: Read literally, “no recognized environmental conditions requiring
remediation or further investigation” is satisfied (there are no RECs, and no
further investigation is recommended), so the CP is arguably met. But a closing
file that contains a Phase I identifying a CREC and no Phase II needs a clear,
written record of why that was acceptable. Recommendation: place a CP
satisfaction/waiver memorandum in the closing file expressly recording the
January 22, 2025 waiver, the NFA letter, the institutional controls, and the
mitigants in I-2 and I-3. This is a file-integrity point, not a drafting point, but it is
the kind of item that surfaces in an examination two years later.

I-2 (High) — The Land Use Restriction covenants and the LUR default
are now in the Mortgage, but the Environmental Indemnity must mirror
them.

addressing the LUR, “including the vapor barrier maintenance and periodic
inspection obligation and the prohibition on residential use of the ground floor,”

restriction”); Schedule B-I Requirement 6 (same requirements for the
Environmental Indemnity); Phase I ESA §§5.3, 5.4, 6(d); Appraisal §5.

prohibition on residential use of the Bay 1 ground floor (§11.1(a)); vapor barrier

(§11.1(b)); annual inspection by a licensed environmental professional (plus

{"file_path": "response.md", "content": "# Deliverables

Two documents were produced from the eight source documents in `documents/`:

1. **`mortgage-and-security-agreement.docx`** — a recordable-form South Carolina
   Mortgage and Security Agreement (with absolute assignment of leases and rents and
   fixture filing), 18 articles, 127 sections, 5 exhibits and a lease schedule, 59 pages.
2. **`drafting-issues-memorandum.docx`** — the accompanying issues memorandum, with a
   top-risk register, a full figure-reconciliation schedule, issue-by-issue analysis
   (63 numbered items across 12 subject areas), a table of drafting resolutions adopted,
   and open items / diligence requests, 37 pages.

# Basis

The Term Sheet dated April 1, 2025 was treated as the controlling commercial instrument.
Every figure and date in the record was recomputed from its components; every
cross-reference in the Mortgage was machine-checked (127 sections, 18 articles, no
unresolved references).

# Principal findings recorded in the memorandum

- **The appraisal is internally irreconcilable.** Its stated income approach ($338,000
  as-is NOI at 6.25%; $587,000 stabilized at 5.85%) supports roughly $5.4m and $10.0m
  against concluded values of $18.2m and $23.5m — implied cap rates of 1.86% and 2.50%.
- **Occupancy is 56.13% (17,400 SF), not the 68% / 21,400 SF** recited in the Term Sheet
  and the appraisal; the error is embedded in the appraisal's rent and vacancy analysis.
- **The 1.25x DSCR covenant is unachievable** on the record's own projections: 0.55x
  amortizing / 0.72x interest-only in the best-case stabilization (NOI of $1,405,299
  would be required), so the covenant generates its own Event of Default at the first test.
- **The interest-shortfall guaranty expires at month 14; DSCR testing begins at month 24**,
  leaving ~$457,000 of projected unfunded debt service in the gap.
- **The 10% retainage required by Term Sheet §8.4 is absent from the draw schedule**
  (~$225,000 overstatement of contractor cash), and the draw schedule does not reconcile
  to the budget detail ($50,000 HVAC / $50,000 elevator reallocation, $5,000 overrun).
- **The Anson Lane strip** was conveyed by quitclaim, the title insurer reserves the right
  to limit coverage by endorsement, and the title commitment and Phase I ESA describe the
  strip's extent differently.
- **Sources and uses are ~$352,075 short** of closing costs and required closing-date reserves.

# Drafting resolutions flagged for instruction

Where the record was ambiguous the memorandum records the resolution adopted and its
authority — notably the yield-maintenance formula (the 1.00% floor was retained from the
Term Sheet, and the 50 bp placement departed from it under supervision instruction),
the DSCR first-test date, the net worth covenant obligor, and the additions beyond the
Term Sheet (change of control, independent manager, LUR covenants, DSCR cure reserve,
DACA, pari passu equity funding).
"}
